props.title: Shivers

sections.content: David Cronenberg's feature debut Shivers (1975) established his signature body horror style that would influence decades of visceral cinema. This apartment-set nightmare about parasitic organisms turning residents into sex-crazed zombies shocked audiences with its blend of exploitation elements and serious scientific horror. The film's themes of sexual liberation gone wrong reflected cultural anxieties of the 1970s sexual revolution, while its confined setting and viral outbreak narrative prefigured later classics like [REC] (2007) and 28 Days Later (2002).

sections.content: The film's influence on parasitic body horror remains evident in works like Slither (2006) and The Faculty (1998). Cronenberg's clinical approach to body transformation horror would reach its apex in The Fly (1986), but Shivers established his core interests in sexuality, disease, and social collapse. The sterile high-rise setting creates an effective contrast with the primal chaos unleashed within, a technique later echoed in films like High-Rise (2015).

Beyond its immediate horror impact, Shivers helped establish Canadian genre cinema as a serious artistic force. Along with Bob Clark's Black Christmas (1974), it proved Canadian horror could compete internationally. The film's modest budget ($179,000) led to creative practical effects solutions that influenced later independent horror filmmakers like Stuart Gordon (Re-Animator (1985)) and Frank Henenlotter (Basket Case (1982)). movies.title: Videodrome
movies.slug: Cronenberg's masterpiece about media consumption and technological body horror

sections.content: Contemporary body horror films like Titane (2021) and Possessor (2020) carry clear DNA from Shivers' bold mixing of sexuality and corporeal transformation. Brandon Cronenberg, David's son, particularly channels the clinical-yet-visceral approach pioneered in Shivers. The film's themes of contagion and social breakdown within confined spaces continue to resonate in recent works like The Sadness (2021) and Mayhem (2017).
